newsitem.title: USA: New U.S. defense secretary to visit Europe.
newsitem.headline: New U.S. defense secretary to visit Europe.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen will visit NATO headquarters in Brussels and also go to Germany, Bosnia and Italy March 4-7 on his first foreign trip, the Pentagon said on Friday.

Cohen, who replaced William Perry as defence secretary last month, will depart on the night of March 3 and fly first to NATO headquarters for talks on March 4 with U.S. and other officials. Later in the week he will visit U.S. peacekeeping troops in Bosnia.

The former senator from Maine and only Republican member of President Bill Clinton's Cabinet will also hold talks in Bonn with German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe and in Rome with Italian Defence Minister Beniamini Andreatta.
Cohen will fly home from Rome on March 7.

The United States has committed up to 8,500 troops as part of a NATO-led peacekeeping force in Bosnia, and Pentagon officials said Cohen wanted to visit with some of those troops as one of his first overseas tasks.

Cohen, selected by Clinton when the popular Perry quit the job after three years as secretary, has vowed that U.S. troops will be out of Bosnia in mid-1998 as scheduled and will not return, even if European countries decide that more peacekeeping is needed in that torn country.

During his brief visit to Brussels on March 4, Cohen will meet with the permanent U.S. representative to NATO and with members of the American mission there. He could meet with other officials although no firm schedule was announced.

During his visit to Germany, Cohen will also meet with senior U.S. military officials in Stuttgart and also visit American troops at military training areas at Hohenfelds and Grafenwoehr, according to defence officials.

Among issues he is expected to discuss with military leaders there is a probe of sexual harassment at a U.S. training centre in Darmstadt, where three male instructors are alleged to have raped and sodomized female soldiers.
The U.S. Army said on Thursday the male commander of the training centre had been replaced with a woman.

The Army has already been hit by a major sexual harassment scandal at Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland and other domestic training bases, and 11 women soldiers at Darmstadt have now alleged that they were sexually assaulted or harassed by male sergeants from last November to January.
Army officials have conceded that some of the alleged incidents in Darmstadt occurred after a special panel was set up to probe the extent of sexual abuse in the army around the world.
